consensus_summary: Across all four blind responses, justice is a core attribute of God and a covenant demand on His people: rightly ordered relationships, impartial judgment, and active protection/restoration of the vulnerable (Micah 6:8; Amos 5:24; Isaiah 1:17; Psalm 89:14). All note the lexical overlap of mishpat/tsedaqah and Greek dikaiosyne with 'righteousness,' and list retributive judgment, forensic justification, liberationist, covenant-faithfulness, and virtue readings as alternatives of varying prominence.
book_summary: The book defines justice as righteousness applied to right a neighbor who has been wronged — the right Way to live — noting that English translations often render the same Hebrew righteousness word as 'justice' in such contexts (e.g., KJV Gen 18:19; Ps 89:14).
consensus_core_identification: Justice = God's righteous character and its demanded human counterpart: right judgment and rightly ordered relationships, including both impartial/retributive judgment and restorative protection of the vulnerable.
book_core_identification: Justice = righteousness in restorative action toward a wronged neighbor; lexically the same Hebrew righteousness word, translated 'justice' when applied interpersonally to set a wrong right.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts justice to the restorative, neighbor-directed application of righteousness ('righting a wronged neighbor'), effectively excluding or sidelining the retributive/judicial-penalty sense, the forensic justification-by-faith sense, and justice as abstract impartial adjudication — all of which the consensus admits as part of or alongside the core. The book also makes the lexical identity with 'righteousness' definitional rather than an incidental translation overlap.
rationale: The book's central referent remains within the consensus category: justice as covenant righteousness enacted in right relationships, with special concern for the wronged/oppressed — essentially the consensus primary meaning (Micah 6:8, Isaiah 1:17, Jer 22:3 territory) plus the consensus's own note that Hebrew righteousness vocabulary is rendered 'justice' in English. There is no replacement of the referent, so it is not DIVERGENT, and it is clearly covered by consensus, so not NOVEL. However, defining justice exclusively as restorative righteousness toward a wronged neighbor materially narrows the extension by dropping retributive and forensic cases the consensus includes, so it exceeds mere rewording and is REFINED rather than MATCH.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH: the book's definition is simply a compressed version of the consensus primary meaning (restorative, relational righteousness) and its lexical note mirrors the consensus's own observation about tsedaqah/dikaiosyne; the omission of retributive and forensic senses in a short glossary entry may be brevity rather than deliberate exclusion.
